questions.q: Put in order from broadest to most granular: which of these is the correct sequence of the four layers of Salesforce data security?
options: Org access, object-level security, field-level security, record-level security
Record-level security, field-level security, object-level security, org access
Field-level security, record-level security, org access, object-level security
Object-level security, record-level security, field-level security, org access
questions.explain: Org access (can you log in at all) is broadest, then object-level (can you see this object at all), then field-level (can you see this field on a visible object), then record-level (can you see this specific record).

questions.q: A sharing rule attempts to grant a group of users access to records they currently can't see. Organization-wide default for the object is already Public Read/Write. What happens?
options: The sharing rule fails validation and can't be saved
The sharing rule has no effect, since those users already have the access it would grant
The sharing rule silently narrows access instead
Salesforce automatically changes the OWD to Private first
questions.explain: Sharing rules only ever add access on top of OWD. If OWD already grants Read/Write to everyone, a sharing rule trying to grant the same or lesser access has nothing left to add.

questions.q: Which of the five classic record-visibility mechanisms is a one-off, user-initiated grant on a single record rather than an automated or structural grant?
options: Role hierarchy
Organization-wide defaults
Sharing rules
Manual sharing
questions.explain: Manual sharing is the only one of the five classic mechanisms that a specific user triggers by hand, record by record, rather than something that runs automatically off role membership, group membership, or record criteria.

questions.q: An architect is unsure whether a new custom object's OWD should be Private or Public Read Only. Why does this course recommend starting with the more restrictive option?
options: Public Read Only is not a valid OWD setting for custom objects
Widening OWD later is comparatively low-risk, while tightening it later forces re-auditing every sharing rule, team, and manual share built on top of the looser default
Private is required by Salesforce for any object with more than one record type
Record-level security has no effect until OWD is set to Private first
questions.explain: Starting private and widening deliberately is the safer direction because loosening OWD later is low-risk, but tightening it later is a breaking change — every sharing mechanism layered on top of the old, looser default now has to be re-examined.

questions.q: Which requirement can none of the five classic sharing mechanisms satisfy on their own, requiring Restriction Rules or Scoping Rules instead?
options: Granting a manager visibility into their team's records
Granting one specific user temporary access to a single record
Narrowing what a user can see below what organization-wide defaults already grant them
Granting a group of users access to records matching a specific criteria
questions.explain: Every classic mechanism (OWD, role hierarchy, sharing rules, manual sharing, teams) can only add access on top of OWD, never take it away. Narrowing visibility below OWD needs a genuinely different kind of control — a visibility filter, which is what Restriction Rules and Scoping Rules provide.
